1977075.extract:
Brancaster is a village and civil parish on the north coast of the English county Norfolk. It is about 3 miles (4.8 km) west of the town Burnham Market, 22 miles (35 km) north of the town King's Lynn and 31 miles (50 km) north-west of the city Norwich. The parish includes the villages Brancaster and Brancaster Staithe and the former parish Burnham Deepdale, all of which lie along the A149 road. The Roman settlement Branodunum is on the edge of the village Brancaster.
The parish has an area of 8.27 square miles (21.4 km2) and at the 2011 census had a population of 797 in 406 households. For the purposes of local government, the parish falls within the district King's Lynn and West Norfolk. It is on the North Sea coast, with the villages bordering Brancaster Manor marshes. Scolt Head Island, a barrier island designated as a National Nature Reserve within the neighbouring parish Burnham Norton, is immediately to the north of much the parish boundary.

'''Brancaster''' is a village and [[civil parish]] on the north coast of the English county [[Norfolk]]. It is about {{convert|3|mi|km}} west of the town [[Burnham Market]], {{convert|22|mi|km}} north of the town [[King's Lynn]] and {{convert|31|mi|km}} north-west of the city [[Norwich]]. The parish includes the villages Brancaster and Brancaster Staithe and the former parish [[Burnham Deepdale]], all of which lie along the [[A149 road]]. The Roman settlement [[Branodunum]] is on the edge of the village Brancaster.

The parish has an area of {{convert|8.27|mi2|km2}} and at the [[United Kingdom Census 2001|2011 census]] had a population of 797 in 406 households. For the purposes of local government, the parish falls within the [[Non-metropolitan district|district]] [[King's Lynn and West Norfolk]]. It is on the [[North Sea]] coast, with the villages bordering [[Brancaster Manor]] marshes. [[Scolt Head Island]], a [[barrier island]] designated as a [[National Nature Reserve]] within the neighbouring parish [[Burnham Norton]], is immediately to the north of much the parish boundary.

==History==
{{main|Branodunum}}
The [[Roman Britain|Roman]] fort and settlement [[Branodunum]] is immediately to the east of the modern village of Brancaster. Built in around CE 230 to protect the approaches to [[The Wash]], it later became part of the network of [[Saxon Shore forts]] protecting Roman Britain from attack by raiding forces. The fort was originally built with a harbour. The Roman-period shoreline is now inland.

[[File:SS Vina, The Brancaster Wreck.jpg|thumb|The wreck of the SS ''Vina'' (2010)]]
The wreck of the [[Coastal trading vessel|coaster]] SS ''Vina'', which was used for target practice by the [[Royal Air Force]] before accidentally sinking in 1944, is visible at low tide on sand dunes. The ship dragged her anchor on 20 August 1944 in a north-westerly gale and ran ashore.

During the 1950s and '60s, Brancaster was considered as a possible location for the launch site for the [[British space programme]].<ref>[http://www.bbc.co.uk/norfolk/your/extra/space.shtml "Norfolk's place in the space race" BBC Norfolk] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050126233853/http://www.bbc.co.uk/norfolk/your/extra/space.shtml |date=26 January 2005 }}</ref>

==Geography==
[[File:RWNGC clubhouse at high tide - geograph.org.uk - 126695.jpg|thumb|RWNGC clubhouse at high tide]]
The [[Royal West Norfolk Golf Club]], founded in 1892, is located on the coastal section of the parish. The course was laid out by [[Horace Hutchinson]], but due to the fragility of the coastline it has undergone many changes.<ref name="GravesCornish2002">{{cite book|last1=Graves|first1=Robert Muir|last2=Cornish|first2=Geoffrey S.|title=Classic Golf Hole Design: Using the Greatest Holes as Inspiration for Modern Courses|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jq4hmzS4oIcC&pg=PA65|date=29 October 2002|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-471-43129-9|page=65}}</ref> At high tide the course can become an island, with parts of it inaccessible.<ref name="Lyall2014">{{cite book|last=Lyall|first=Ian|title=Explore the North Norfolk Coast|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aXS9BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA18|date=8 May 2014|publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-1-291-82069-0|page=18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://golf.com/travel/best-hole-royal-west-norfolk-no-8/|title=The best hole I ever played: This amazing par-5’s fairway is dictated by the tides|first1=Thomas|last1=Brown|work=Golf Magazine|date=1 August 2020}}</ref>  In 2014 it was listed as the 47th best golf course in the UK and Ireland by ''[[Golf Monthly]]'' magazine.

Much of the coastal section of the parish, including [[Brancaster Manor]] marshes, are managed by the [[National Trust]]. The [[Norfolk Coast Path]] long distance footpath runs through the parish. A [[petrified forest]] can be seen on the foreshore near Brancaster at low tide, about {{convert|3/4|mi}} west of the golf clubhouse. It consists of material similar to compacted peat or [[lignite]]. Fragments wash ashore after storms.
[[File:Brancaster Roman Fort in Norfolk.jpg|thumb|A [[lidar]] view of the site of Brancaster Roman fort]]

==Governance==
An [[Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom|electoral ward]] in the same name exists. This ward had a population at the 2011 census of 1,293.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=13693577&c=Brancaster&d=14&e=62&g=6449038&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1440673465297&enc=1|title=Ward population 2011|access-date=27 August 2015}}</ref>

==Notable people==
*[[John Brancastre]] (died 1218), churchman and administrator, was Vicar of Brancaster and was probably born in the village.
*[[John Weatherhead]] (1775–1797), Royal Navy officer, was born here, son of a Rector
*[[William Bolton (Royal Navy officer, died 1830)|Captain Sir William Bolton]] (1777–1830), Royal Navy officer, grew up at Brancaster, where his father was Rector.
*[[Herbert Reeve]] (1868–1956), Rector of Brancaster 1924 to 1945
*[[Felicity Tree]] (1894–1978), socialite daughter of [[Herbert Beerbohm Tree]], lived at Brancaster

2876230.title: Felbrigg Hall
2876230.extract: Felbrigg Hall is a 17th-century English country house near the village of that name in Norfolk. Part of a National Trust property, the unaltered 17th-century house is noted for its Jacobean architecture and fine Georgian interior. Outside is a walled garden, an orangery and orchards. The house and grounds were bequeathed to the National Trust in 1969 by Robert Ketton-Cremer. The hall is Grade I on the National Heritage List for England. Most of the grounds are part of Felbrigg Woods, a Site of Special Scientific Interest.

'''Felbrigg Hall''' is a 17th-century [[English country house]] near [[Felbrigg|the village of that name]] in Norfolk.<ref>''OS Explorer Map 24'' (Edition A 1997) – ''Norfolk Coast Central''. {{ISBN|0-319-21726-4}}.</ref> Part of a [[National Trust]] property, the unaltered 17th-century house is noted for its [[Jacobean architecture]] and fine [[Georgian architecture|Georgian interior]]. Outside is a [[walled garden]], an [[orangery]] and orchards. The house and grounds were bequeathed to the National Trust in 1969 by [[Robert Ketton-Cremer]]. The hall is [[Listed building#Categories of listed building|Grade I]] on the [[National Heritage List for England]].<ref name=NHLEHouse>{{NHLE |num=1373644 |desc=Felbrigg Hall |access-date=23 December 2016 |mode=cs2}}</ref> Most of the grounds are part of [[Felbrigg Woods]], a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]].

==History==
The estate originated with the Felbrigg family. It passed to John Wyndham (died 1475) and remained in that family for centuries.

[[Thomas Wyndham of Felbrigg|Thomas Wyndham (died 1522)]] was a councillor to King [[Henry VIII]].<ref>[http://www.hamline.edu/brass/pdfs/y_felb_1608_engr_1611-12.pdf Hamline University (accessed Oct 2010)]{{dead link |date=January 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref> Later, residents included [[John Wyndham (1558–1645)]] who was probably the builder of Felbrigg Hall. The last Wyndham or Windham of Felbrigg was William Wyndham (died 1810). Much land had been added to the medieval estate in the 17th and 18th centuries.<ref>Historic England [https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000185 Retrieved 5 August 2017.]</ref> 
Above the entablature the family arms and the projecting bays bear the words GLORIA DEO IN EXCELSIS in pierced stone, surmounted by heraldic beasts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.heritage.norfolk.gov.uk/record-details?MNF6633-Felbrigg-Hall&Index=6105&RecordCount=57339&SessionID=e36fb366-2f2d-4e45-a918-acf04feba925.|title = Felbrigg-Hall - Norfolk Heritage Explorer}}</ref><ref>http://www.literarynorfolk.co.uk/felbrigg.htm. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161108104304/http://www.literarynorfolk.co.uk/felbrigg.htm |date=8 November 2016 }}</ref>

The last owner of the house, before it passed into National Trust ownership, was [[Robert Wyndham Ketton-Cremer]]. His heir, his brother Richard, was killed in action in the [[Second World War]]. Robert's memorial to Richard is in the woods behind the house.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

Robert Wyndham Ketton-Cremer wrote a number of books, particularly about Norfolk, including ''Felbrigg: the Story of a House'',<ref>[https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/6325329 WorldCat OCLC Number: 6325329]</ref> and ''Norfolk in the Civil War'', Faber, 1969.<ref>[https://www.amazon.co.uk/Norfolk-Civil-War-R-W-Ketton-Cremer/dp/057109130X Norfolk in the Civil War] Retrieved 10 August 2013.</ref> Robert Ketton-Cremer never married, and with no heirs, left the estate to the National Trust on his death in 1969. Part of the estate was acquired by [[Beeston Hall School]].

Christopher Mackie was the administrator, or houseman, of Felbrigg Hall until 1990. His wife [[Mary Mackie]] wrote three books on their experiences there: ''Cobwebs and Cream Teas'', ''Dry Rot and Daffodils'' and ''Frogspawn and Floor Polish''.<ref>British Library search under "Mary Mackie" [http://explore.bl.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/search.do?fn=search&ct=search&initialSearch=true&mode=Basic&tab=local_tab&indx=1&dum=true&srt=rank&vid=BLVU1&frbg=&tb=t&vl%28freeText0%29=Mary+Mackie&scp.scps=scope%3A%28BLCONTENT%29&vl%28488279563UI0%29=any&vl%28488279563UI0%29=title&vl%28488279563UI0%29=any Retrieved 4 August 2017.]</ref>

==Today==
Today the Felbrigg estate covers approximately 1,760 [[acre]]s (about 7 km<sup>2</sup>) of parkland including the {{convert|520|acre|km2|adj=on}} of Great Wood, which shelters the house. There is public access to the grounds along a number of [[waymarking|waymarked]] walks through the estate, including the [[Weavers' Way]] [[long-distance footpath]].<ref>[http://www.countrysideaccess.norfolk.gov.uk/walk.aspx?section=1&id=71 Norfolk long distance footpaths] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130723001532/http://www.countrysideaccess.norfolk.gov.uk/walk.aspx?section=1&id=71 |date=23 July 2013}} Retrieved 6 August 2013</ref> [[National Cycle Network]] regional routes 33 and 30 also pass through the estate.<ref>[http://www.sustrans.org.uk/ncn/map/route/wells-holkham-circuit Sustrans] Retrieved 9 August 2013</ref>

==The gardens==
Felbrigg garden is laid out in two different styles. The west garden is laid out in the style of a typical [[Victorian era|Victorian]] [[pleasure ground]], arranged around an 18th-century [[orangery]]. Accentuating the play between light and shade, its [[Lawn#The English lawn|formal lawn]]s are interspersed with areas of dark shrubbery. This garden features a number of specimens from North America including [[Erythrobalanus|red oaks]], [[Thuja plicata|western red cedar]]s, and a meadow with a [[walled garden]]. There are double borders of mixed shrubs, a [[herbaceous border]], and more. The orchard has been planted with varieties of fruit known to have grown in the garden during the 19th century. The gardens are home to the [[NCCPG National Plant Collection|National Collection]] of [[colchicum]]s.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

The gardens are Grade II* listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]]<ref name=NHLEGarden>{{NHLE |num=1000185 |desc=Felbrigg Hall |access-date=23 December 2016 |mode=cs2}}</ref> and [[Felbrigg Woods]] is a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]].<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://designatedsites.naturalengland.org.uk/SiteDetail.aspx?SiteCode=S1001767&SiteName=&countyCode=29&responsiblePerson=&SeaArea=&IFCAArea= |title=Designated Sites View: Felbrigg Woods |series=Sites of Special Scientific Interest |publisher=Natural England |accessdate=16 May 2018}}</ref>

==National Trust controversy==
To mark the 50th anniversary of the [[Sexual Offences Act 1967|decriminalisation of sexual activity between men]] in England and Wales, the National Trust in summer 2017 organised a "Prejudice and Pride" campaign highlighting the [[LGBT]] themes in its properties. At Felbrigg Hall, a short film narrated by [[Stephen Fry]] stated that Robert Wyndham Ketton-Cremer had been widely known to be [[homosexual]],<ref>{{Cite web |title= The unfinished portrait |website = [[YouTube]]|url=https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=pdgaAdhapoc|date=21 July 2017}}{{cbignore}}{{Dead Youtube links|date=February 2022}}</ref> though others claimed that this was only known by his close friends.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Trust volunteers refusing to wear gay pride lanyards in protest over 'outing' former lord of the manor |author=Lucy Pasha-Robinson |website=The Independent |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/national-trust-felbrigg-hall-norfolk-gay-pride-lanyards-lgbt-lord-manor-robert-wyndham-ketton-cremer-a7876321.html |date=4 August 2017}}</ref> Two of Ketton-Cremer's godchildren criticised the decision, claiming that a public [[outing]] would have been against Ketton-Cremer's wishes and accusing the Trust of using their godfather to generate publicity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Trust criticised for "outing" country squire |website=The Telegraph |date=29 July 2017 |author=Steve Bird |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/07/28/national-trust-criticised-outing-country-squire/}}</ref>

The Trust also requested that volunteers wear a badge featuring the charity's logo atop the colours of the [[Rainbow flag (LGBT movement)|LGBT pride flag]]. Of the house's 350 volunteers, ten refused and were asked to take backstage roles during the campaign.<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Trust volunteers refuse to wear LGBTQ badges |date=4 August 2017 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-norfolk-40825660 |website=BBC News}}</ref> Sections of the press called on the Trust to reverse its decision,<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Trust reverses decision enforcing use of gay pride badges |author=Jamie Grierson |date=5 August 2017 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2017/aug/05/national-trust-reverses-decision-on-gay-pride-badges |website=The Guardian}}</ref> and some members cancelled their membership over the issue.<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Trust facing membership boycott over gay campaign |author=Steve Bird |date=4 August 2017 |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/08/04/national-trust-facing-membership-boycott-gay-campaign/ |website=The Telegraph}}</ref> The Trust subsequently U-turned on the wearing of badges.<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Trust U-turn over LGBTQ badges at Felbrigg Hall |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-norfolk-40837709 |website=BBC News |date=5 August 2017}}</ref>

'''Oxburgh Hall''' is a [[moat]]ed [[country house]] in [[Oxborough]], [[Norfolk]], [[England]]. The hall was built for Sir Edmund Bedingfeld who obtained a [[licence to crenellate]] in 1482. The [[Bedingfeld Baronets|Bedingfelds]] gained the [[Lord of the Manor|manor]] of Oxborough through marriage in the early 15th century, and the family has lived at the hall since its construction, although ownership passed to the [[National Trust]] in 1952. The house underwent extensive refurbishment in the mid 19th century under [[John Chessell Buckler]] and [[Augustus Pugin]].

==History==
[[Image:Oxburgh-gatehouse-inside.jpg|thumb|left|150px|The courtyard front of the gatehouse, with paired polygonal stair towers]]
An example of a late medieval, inward-facing great house, Oxburgh stands within a square moat about 75 metres on each side, and was originally enclosed; the hall range facing the [[gatehouse]] was pulled down in 1772 for Sir Richard Bedingfeld, providing a more open U-shaped house, with the open end of the U facing south. The entrance, reached by a three-arched bridge on the north side, is through a fortified gatehouse, described by [[Nikolaus Pevsner]] as "the most prominent of the English brick gatehouses of the 15th century".{{sfn|Pevsner|Wilson|2002|pp=584-588}} The gate was designed to evoke the owner's power and prestige, though as fortification its value is largely symbolic; it is flanked by tall polygonal towers rising in seven tiers, with symmetrical wings extending either side that reveal nothing on the exterior of their differing internal arrangements. 

About 1835 the open end of the U was filled in with a picturesque, by no means archaeologically correct range that recreated the central courtyard.{{sfn|Pevsner|Wilson|2002|pp=584-588}} Other Victorian additions include the [[Flanders|Flemish]]-style stepped gables, the massive southeast tower, the  oriel windows overhanging the moat and [[terracotta]] chimneys. Four towers were added to the walled kitchen garden. In the 1830s under [[Sir Henry Paston-Bedingfeld, 6th Baronet]], [[John Chessell Buckler]] and [[Augustus Pugin]] were commissioned to restore and develop the hall.<ref name="NHLE">{{NHLE| num=1342586|desc=Oxburgh Hall|grade=I|access-date=16 December 2014}}</ref> A chapel was added, and the walled kitchen garden and flower gardens were rebuilt. A stable block was also added.<ref name="NHLEGarden">{{NHLE|num=1001010|desc=Oxburgh Hall park and garden|grade=II|access-date=17 April 2020}}</ref>

The hall is known for its [[priest hole]], constructed by [[Nicholas Owen (Jesuit)|Nicholas Owen]]. The [[Roman Catholic Church|Catholic]] Bedingfelds constructed the closet, accessed through a lavatory, to enable the concealment of priests.{{sfn|Garnett|2000|p=25}} The hall is also notable for the [[Oxburgh Hangings]], needlework hangings by [[Mary, Queen of Scots]] and [[Bess of Hardwick]]. Mary worked on these while imprisoned in England, in the custody of the [[Earl of Shrewsbury]].{{sfn|Garnett|2000|pp=21-22}}

A landscape park was laid out to the south and west of the house in the 1830s. A French [[parterre]] was laid out to the east of the moat at this time and a pleasure ground to the west of the new chapel was also created.<ref name="NHLEGarden"/> The estate has a number of woodland walks, including a 'Woodland Explorer' trail.

Oxburgh Hall and the remaining estate was auctioned in lots in 1950. The Hall and gardens faced demolition in 1951, but were saved when Sybil, Lady Bedingfeld, her daughter Mrs Frances Playford, and niece Mrs Violet Hartcup raised enough funds to buy Oxburgh back, then gave it to the [[National Trust]] in 1952.{{sfn|Garnett|2000|p=47}}

In 2021, the Trust announced plans for the reversion of the 175 acres of land at Oxburgh from farmland back to wildlife-friendly woods and  pasture.<ref>{{Cite web|date=7 May 2021|title=National Trust to recreate 19th-century Norfolk woodland using RAF photos|url=http://www.theguardian.com/environment/2021/may/07/national-trust-to-recreate-19th-century-norfolk-woodland-using-raf-photos|work=The Guardian}}</ref> The project will be informed by the use of photographs taken during an [[Royal Air Force|RAF]] aerial survey in 1946 and will see the planting of 227 trees to recreate habitats for local wildlife.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Oxburgh Hall: Photos from 1946 help restore Tudor manor parkland|publisher=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-norfolk-57009271|access-date=11 May 2021}}</ref>

==Architecture and description==
The hall has been [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed Grade I]] on the [[National Heritage List for England]] since 1951. This is the highest level of designation.<ref name="NHLE"/> The landscaped and formal gardens of the hall have been Grade II listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]] since 1987.<ref name="NHLEGarden"/>

3619725.title: The Hardmans' House
3619725.extract:
The Hardmans' House, at 59 Rodney Street, Liverpool, Merseyside, England, is a National Trust property and home of the "E. Chambré Hardman Studio, House & Photographic Collection". The property was acquired by the National Trust in 2003.
The house is a Georgian terraced house which served as both the studio and home of photographer E. Chambré Hardman from 1947 to 1988, and his wife, business partner and fellow photographer, Margaret until her death in 1969. On display are an extensive collection of photographs, the studio where most were taken, as well as the darkroom where they were developed and printed.
The collection consists of portraits of the people of Liverpool, their city and the landscapes of the surrounding countryside.

5335922.title: Blakeney Point
5335922.extract:
Blakeney Point (designated as Blakeney National Nature Reserve) is a national nature reserve situated near to the villages of Blakeney, Morston and Cley next the Sea on the north coast of Norfolk, England. Its main feature is a 6.4 km (4.0 mi) spit of shingle and sand dunes, but the reserve also includes salt marshes, tidal mudflats and reclaimed farmland. It has been managed by the National Trust since 1912, and lies within the North Norfolk Coast Site of Special Scientific Interest, which is additionally protected through Natura 2000, Special Protection Area (SPA), International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Ramsar listings. The reserve is part of both an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB), and a World Biosphere Reserve. The Point has been studied for more than a century, following pioneering ecological studies by botanist Francis Wall Oliver and a bird ringing programme initiated by ornithologist Emma Turner.
The area has a long history of human occupation; ruins of a medieval monastery and "Blakeney Chapel" (probably a domestic dwelling) are buried in the marshes. The towns sheltered by the shingle spit were once important harbours, but land reclamation schemes starting in the 17th century resulted in the silting up of the river channels. The reserve is important for breeding birds, especially terns, and its location makes it a major site for migrating birds in autumn. Up to 500 seals may gather at the end of the spit, and its sand and shingle hold a number of specialised invertebrates and plants, including the edible samphire, or "sea asparagus".
The many visitors who come to birdwatch, sail or for other outdoor recreations are important to the local economy, but the land-based activities jeopardize nesting birds and fragile habitats, especially the dunes. Some access restrictions on humans and dogs help to reduce the adverse effects, and trips to see the seals are usually undertaken by boat. The spit is a dynamic structure, gradually moving towards the coast and extending to the west. Land is lost to the sea as the spit rolls forward. The River Glaven can become blocked by the advancing shingle and cause flooding of Cley village, Cley Marshes nature reserve, and the environmentally important reclaimed grazing pastures, so the river has to be realigned every few decades.

'''Blakeney Point''' (designated as '''Blakeney National Nature Reserve''') is a [[National nature reserves in England|national nature reserve]] situated near to the villages of [[Blakeney, Norfolk|Blakeney]], [[Morston]] and [[Cley next the Sea]] on the north coast of [[Norfolk]], England. Its main feature is a {{convert|6.4|km|mi|abbr=on}} [[spit (landform)|spit]] of [[shingle beach|shingle]] and [[dune|sand dunes]], but the reserve also includes [[salt marsh]]es, tidal mudflats and reclaimed farmland. It has been managed by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 1912, and lies within the [[North Norfolk Coast Site of Special Scientific Interest]], which is additionally protected through [[Natura 2000]], [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA), [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] (IUCN) and [[Ramsar Convention|Ramsar]] listings. The reserve is part of both an [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] (AONB), and a [[World Network of Biosphere Reserves|World Biosphere Reserve]]. The Point has been studied for more than a century, following pioneering [[ecology|ecological]] studies by botanist [[Francis Wall Oliver]] and a [[bird ringing]] programme initiated by ornithologist [[Emma Turner (photographer)|Emma Turner]].

The area has a long history of human occupation; ruins of a [[medieval]] [[monastery]] and "[[Blakeney Chapel]]" (probably a domestic dwelling) are buried in the marshes. The towns sheltered by the shingle spit were once important harbours, but [[land reclamation]] schemes starting in the 17th century resulted in the silting up of the river channels. The reserve is important for breeding birds, especially [[tern]]s, and its location makes it a major site for [[bird migration|migrating birds]] in autumn. Up to 500 [[pinniped|seals]] may gather at the end of the spit, and its sand and shingle hold a number of specialised [[invertebrate]]s and plants, including the edible [[Salicornia europaea|samphire]], or "sea asparagus".

The many visitors who come to [[birdwatching|birdwatch]], [[sailing|sail]] or for other outdoor recreations are important to the local economy, but the land-based activities jeopardize nesting birds and fragile [[habitat]]s, especially the dunes. Some access restrictions on humans and dogs help to reduce the adverse effects, and trips to see the seals are usually undertaken by boat. The spit is a dynamic structure, gradually moving towards the coast and extending to the west. Land is lost to the sea as the spit rolls forward. The [[River Glaven]] can become blocked by the advancing shingle and cause flooding of Cley village, [[Cley Marshes]] nature reserve, and the environmentally important reclaimed grazing pastures, so the river has to be realigned every few decades.

==Description==
[[File:Blakeney National Nature Reserve, Norfolk, England-14Sept2011.jpg|right|thumb|[[Norfolk Coast Path]] goes along the top of a portion of the sea wall. The salt marshes are on the left and farmland is on the right.]]
Blakeney Point, like most of the northern part of the marshes in this area, is part of the parish of [[Cley next the Sea]].<ref name=wrightchap>{{cite journal | last= Wright | first= John | year= 1999 | title= The chapel on Blakeney Eye: some documentary evidence | journal= Glaven Historian | volume= 2 | pages= 26–33 | url= http://www.history-blakeney-area.org.uk/GH-Files/GH1-5/GH%202.6.pdf | access-date= 2013-12-01 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131203023140/http://www.history-blakeney-area.org.uk/GH-Files/GH1-5/GH%202.6.pdf | archive-date= 2013-12-03 | url-status= dead }}</ref> The main spit runs roughly west to east, and joins the mainland at Cley Beach before continuing onwards as a coastal ridge to [[Weybourne, Norfolk|Weybourne]]. It is approximately {{convert|6.4|km|mi|abbr=on}} long,<ref name = NTwalk/> and is composed of a shingle bank which in places is {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} in width and up to {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} high. It has been estimated that there are 2.3 million m<sup>3</sup> (82 million ft<sup>3</sup>) of shingle in the spit,<ref>Bridges (1998) p. 39.</ref> 97 per cent of which is derived from [[flint]].<ref name = AM24>Steers, J A in Allison & Morley (1989) p. 24.</ref>

The Point was formed by [[longshore drift]] and this movement continues westward; the spit lengthened by {{convert|132.1|m|ft|abbr=on}} between 1886 and 1925.<ref name =may/> At the western end, the shingle curves south towards the mainland. This feature has developed several times over the years, giving the impression from the air of a series of hooks along the south side of the spit.<ref name= Tansley848>Tansley (1939) pp. 848–849.</ref> [[Salt marshes]] have formed between the shingle curves and in front of the coasts sheltered by the spit,<ref name =may/> and [[dune|sand dunes]] have accumulated at the Point's western end.<ref name = NTwalk/> Some of the shorter side ridges meet the main ridge at a steep angle due to the southward movement of the latter.<ref name = AM19>Steers, J A in Allison & Morley (1989) p. 19.</ref> There is an area of reclaimed farmland, known as Blakeney Freshes, to the west of Cley Beach Road.<ref name = walk/><ref name= carnell/>

[[Norfolk Coast Path]], an ancient [[long distance footpath]], cuts across the south eastern corner of the reserve along the [[seawall|sea wall]] between the farmland and the salt marshes, and further west at [[Holme-next-the-Sea]] the trail joins [[Peddars Way]].<ref name = walk/><ref name = peddar>{{cite web| title= Peddars Way/Norfolk Coast Path| url= http://www.nationaltrail.co.uk/PeddarsWay/| publisher= National Trails}} Retrieved 7 June 2012.</ref> The tip of Blakeney Point can be reached by walking up the shingle spit from the car park at Cley Beach,<ref name = NTwalk/> or by boats from the quay at [[Morston]]. The boat gives good views of the seal colonies and avoids the long walk over a difficult surface.<ref name = NNR/> The National Trust has an information centre and tea room at the quay,<ref name = blakeneynnr>{{cite web| title= Facilities & access | work= Blakeney National Nature Reserve | url= http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/blakeney/facilities-and-access/ | publisher= National Trust }} Retrieved 16 August 2012.</ref> and a visitor centre on the Point. The centre was formerly a [[lifeboat (rescue)|lifeboat]] station and is open in the summer months.<ref name= DK>Dorling Kindersley (2009) p. 214.</ref> Halfway House, or the Watch House, is a building {{convert|2.4|km|mi|abbr=on}} from Cley Beach car park. Originally built in the 19th century as a look-out for [[smuggling|smugglers]], it was used in succession as a [[coast guard]] station, by the [[Girl Guides]], and as a holiday let.<ref name = NTwalk/>
{{clear}}

==History==

===To 1912===
[[File:Blakeney Channel viewed from the top of St Nicholas Church - geograph.org.uk - 1516479.jpg|thumb|alt=view of a river winding through open wetland|The course of the [[River Glaven]] through the mudflats and salt marshes can be seen at low tide.]]
Norfolk has a long history of human occupation dating back to the [[Paleolithic|Palaeolithic]], and has produced many significant [[archaeology|archaeological]] finds. Both [[anatomically modern humans|modern]] and [[Neanderthal]] people were present in the area between 100,000 and 10,000 years ago, before the last [[glacial period|glaciation]], and humans returned as the ice retreated northwards. The archaeological record is poor until about 20,000 years ago, partly because of the very cold conditions that existed then, but also because the coastline was much further north than at present. As the ice retreated during the [[Mesolithic]] (10,000–5,000 BCE), the [[sea level]] rose, filling what is now the [[North Sea]]. This brought the Norfolk coastline much closer to its present line, so that many ancient sites are now under the sea in an area now known as [[Doggerland]].<ref name = coles>{{cite web| author = Coles, Bryony |title= The Doggerland project | work= Research projects | url= http://humanities.exeter.ac.uk/archaeology/research/projects/title_89282_en.html | publisher= University of Exeter}} Retrieved 18 September 2012.</ref><ref name= NAE9>Robertson ''et al.'' (2005) pp. 9–22.</ref> Early Mesolithic flint tools with characteristic [[Blade (archaeology)|long blades]] up to {{convert|15|cm|in|abbr=on}}<ref name= murphy14>Murphy (2009) p. 14.</ref> long found on the present-day coast at [[Titchwell Marsh]] date from a time when it was {{convert|60|–|70|km|mi|abbr=on}} from the sea. Other flint tools have been found dating from the [[Upper Paleolithic]] (50,000–10,000 BCE) to the [[Neolithic]] (5,000–2,500 BCE).<ref name= NAE9/>

An "eye" is an area of higher ground in the marshes, dry enough to support buildings. Blakeney's former [[Carmelites|Carmelite]] [[monastery|friary]], founded in 1296 and [[dissolution of the Monasteries|dissolved]] in 1538, was built in such a location,<ref name= NAE36>Robertson ''et al.'' (2005) p. 36.</ref> and several fragments of plain roof tile and [[pantile (roof material)|pantiles]] dating back to the 13th century have been found near the site of its ruins.<ref name= NAE143>Robertson ''et al.'' (2005) p. 143.</ref>  Originally on the south side of the Glaven, Blakeney Eye had a ditched enclosure during the 11th and 12th centuries, and a building known as "[[Blakeney Chapel]]", which was occupied from the 14th century to around 1600, and again in the late 17th century. Despite its name, it is unlikely that it had a religious function. Nearly a third of the mostly 14th- to 16th-century pottery found within the larger and earlier of the two rooms was imported from the continent,<ref name= lee>{{cite journal| last= Lee | first= Richard | year= 2006 | title = A report on the archaeological excavation of 'Blakeney Chapel' | journal= Glaven Historian | volume= 9 | pages= 3–21 }}</ref><ref name=birks10>Birks (2003) pp. 1–28.</ref> suggesting significant international trade at this time.<ref name= Robinson3>Robinson (2006) pp. 3–5.</ref><ref name = pevsner394>Pevsner & Wilson (2002) pp. 394–397.</ref>

The spit sheltered the [[River Glaven|Glaven ports]], Blakeney, Cley-next-the-Sea and [[Wiveton]], which were important [[medieval]] harbours. Blakeney sent ships to help [[Edward I of England|Edward I's]] war efforts in 1301, and between the 14th and 16th centuries it was the only Norfolk port between [[King's Lynn]] and [[Great Yarmouth]] to have customs officials.<ref name= NAE9/> [[St Nicholas, Blakeney|Blakeney Church]] has a second tower at its east end, an unusual feature in a rural parish church. It has been suggested that it acted as a beacon for mariners,<ref name = BLB>{{cite web| title= Church of St Nicholas, Blakeney | url= http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-222864-church-of-st-nicholas-blakeney | publisher= British Listed Buildings }} Retrieved 10 September 2011.</ref> perhaps by aligning it with the taller west tower to guide ships into the navigable channel between the inlet's sandbanks;<ref name= Robinson3/> that this was not always successful is demonstrated by a number of wrecks in the [[Blakeney Haven|haven]], including a [[Carvel (boat building)|carvel-built]] wooden ship.<ref name= NAE9/>

[[Land reclamation]] schemes, especially those by Henry Calthorpe in 1640 just to the west of Cley, led to the silting up of the Glaven shipping channel and relocation of Cley's [[wharf]].<ref name= pevsner435/> Further enclosure in the mid-1820s aggravated the problem, and also allowed the shingle ridge at the beach to block the former tidal channel to the Salthouse marshes to the east of Cley.<ref name= commission/> In an attempt to halt the decline, [[Thomas Telford]] was consulted in 1822, but his recommendations for reducing the silting were not implemented, and by 1840 almost all of Cley's trade had been lost.<ref name= pevsner435>Pevsner & Wilson (2002) p. 435.</ref> The population stagnated, and the value of all property decreased sharply.<ref name= commission>Hume, Joseph. "[https://books.google.com/books?id=GzQxAQAAMAAJ&dq=%22cley+marshes%22&pg=PA83 Port of Cley and Blakeney]" in appendix to {{cite book | author = Tidal Harbours Commission | title = Second report of the commissioners| year = 1846 | location = London | publisher = W Clowes & Son| pages = 83a–84a}}</ref> Blakeney's shipping trade benefited from the silting up of its nearby rival, and in 1817 the channel to the Haven was deepened to improve access. [[Packet ship]]s ran to [[Kingston upon Hull|Hull]] and [[London]] from 1840, but this trade declined as ships became too large for the harbour.<ref name= pevsner394/>

In the decades preceding [[World War I]], this stretch of coast became famous for its [[waterfowl hunting|wildfowling]]; locals were looking for food, but some more affluent visitors hunted to collect rare birds;<ref name= bishop9>Bishop (1983) pp. 9–13.</ref> Norfolk's first [[barred warbler]] was shot on the point in 1884. In 1901, the Blakeney and Cley Wild Bird Protection Society created a bird sanctuary and appointed as its "watcher", Bob Pinchen, the first of only six men, up to 2012, to hold that post.<ref name= BB100/>

In 1910, the owner of the Point, [[Baron Calthorpe|Augustus Cholmondeley Gough-Calthorpe, 6th Baron Calthorpe]], leased the land to [[University College London]] (UCL), who also purchased the Old Lifeboat House at the end of the spit. When the baron died later that year, his heirs put Blakeney Point up for sale, raising the possibility of development.<ref name = Ayres>Ayres (2012) p. 123.</ref> In 1912, a public appeal initiated by [[Charles Rothschild]] and organised by UCL Professor [[Francis Wall Oliver]] and Dr Sidney Long enabled the purchase of Blakeney Point from the Calthorpe estate, and the land was then donated to the National Trust.<ref name = AM7/> UCL established a research centre at the Old Lifeboat House in 1913,<ref name = NTwalk/> where Oliver and his college pioneered the scientific study of Blakeney Point.<ref name=ucl>{{cite web|title=Blakeney Point |url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/gee/research/blakeney-point |publisher=University College London Department of genetics, evolution and environment |access-date=23 September 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121111000329/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/gee/research/blakeney-point |archive-date=11 November 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> The building is still used by students, and also acts as an information centre.<ref name = NTwalk/> Despite formal protection, the [[tern]] colony was not fenced off until the 1960s.<ref name= BB100>{{cite journal | last= Stubbing | first= Edward | year= 2012 | title= The birds of Blakeney Point: 100 years of National Trust ownership | journal= British Birds | volume= 105 | issue =9 | pages= 520–529 }}</ref>

In 1930, the Point's first "watcher", Bob Pinchen, retired and was replaced by Billy Eales, who had assisted Pinchen the previous summer to "learn the job". His son, Ted Eales, succeeded him as warden when he died in early 1939. Ted Eales went on to work as a wildlife cameraman for [[Anglia Television]] during the winter and served as the Point's warden until retiring in March 1980. Subsequent wardens have included Joe Reed and wildlife presenter [[Ajay Tegala]]. Bob Pinchen, Ted Eales and Ajay Tegala have all written books about their experiences on Blakeney Point as watcher, warden and ranger respectively, the latter being Tegala's ''The Unique Life of a Ranger: Seasons of Change on Blakeney Point''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Blakeney Point: Ajay Tegala on the life of a ranger|url=https://www.discoverwildlife.com/people/blakeney-point-ranger-ajay-tegala|website=Discover Wildlife|date=2022-08-09|access-date=2025-12-01|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Wicken Fen ranger tells unique stories of conservation in new book|url=https://www.cambridgeindependent.co.uk/whats-on/wicken-fen-ranger-tells-unique-stories-of-conservation-in-ne-9271007/|website=Cambridge Independent|date=2022-08-27|access-date=2025-12-01|language=en}}</ref>

The Point was designated as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) in 1954, along with the adjacent [[Cley Marshes]] reserve, and subsumed into the newly created {{convert|7,700|ha|acre|abbr=off|adj=on}} North Norfolk Coast SSSI in 1986. The larger area is now additionally protected through [[Natura 2000]], [[Special Protection Area]] (SPA) and [[Ramsar Convention|Ramsar]] listings, [[IUCN]] category IV (habitat/species management area)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://protectedplanet.net/sites/142734 |publisher=protectedplanet.net |title=Blakeney National Nature Reserve |access-date=23 October 2012}}</ref> and is part of the [[Norfolk Coast AONB|Norfolk Coast Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]].<ref name=encitation>{{cite web |title=North Norfolk Coast |work=SSSI citations |url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001342.pdf |publisher=Natural England |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140202212559/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001342.pdf |archive-date=2014-02-02 }} Retrieved 8 November 2011.</ref> The Point became a [[National Nature Reserve]] (NNR) in 1994,<ref name= whitedjb>{{cite journal| last= White | first= D J B  | year=2005 | title= Blakeney Point and University College London  | journal= The Glaven Historian  | volume= 8 | pages= 17–20 }}</ref> and the coast from Holkham NNR to Salthouse, together with [[Scolt Head Island]], became a [[World Network of Biosphere Reserves|Biosphere Reserve]] in 1976.<ref name = unesco>{{cite web| title= North Norfolk Coast Biosphere Reserve Information | work= UNESCO – Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme Biosphere Reserves Directory | url= http://www.unesco.org/mabdb/br/brdir/directory/biores.asp?code=UKM+09&mode=all | publisher = United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation | access-date = 19 October 2012}}</ref><ref name =liley4>Liley (2008) pp. 4–6.</ref>

==Fauna and flora==

===Birds===
[[File:Chroicocephalus ridibundus.jpg|thumb|alt= grey bird with dark brown head|[[Black-headed gull]]s nest in large numbers on the spit.]]
[[File:Anas penelope -Blakeney National Nature Reserve, Norfolk, England -swimming-8.jpg|right|thumb|A male [[Eurasian wigeon]] swimming at the reserve. Ducks gather at the reserve in winter.]]
Blakeney Point has been designated as one of the most important sites in Europe for nesting terns by the government's [[Joint Nature Conservation Committee]].<ref name=jncccite>{{cite web |title=North Norfolk Coast |work=SPA description |url=http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/page-2008-theme=default |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |access-date=18 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120905153155/http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/page-2008-theme=default |archive-date=5 September 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref> In the early 1900s, the small colonies of [[common tern|common]] and [[little tern]]s were badly affected by egg-taking, disturbance and shooting, but as protection improved the common terns population rose to 2,000 pairs by mid-century, although it subsequently declined to no more than 165 pairs by 2000, perhaps due to predation. [[Sandwich tern]]s were a scarce breeder until the 1970s, but there were 4,000 pairs by 1992. Blakeney is the most important site in Britain for both Sandwich and little terns, the roughly 200 pairs of the latter species amounting to eight per cent of the British population. The 2,000 pairs of [[black-headed gull]]s sharing the breeding area with the terns are believed to protect the colony as a whole from predators like [[red fox]]es. Other nesting birds include about 20 pairs of [[Arctic tern]]s and a few [[Mediterranean gull]]s in the tern colony, [[common ringed plover|ringed plovers]] and [[Eurasian oystercatcher|oystercatchers]] on the shingle and [[common redshank]]s on the salt marsh. The [[wader]]s' breeding success has been compromised by human disturbance and predation by [[gull]]s, [[least weasel|weasels]] and [[stoat]]s, with ringed plovers particularly affected, declining to 12 pairs in 2012 compared to 100 pairs twenty years previously.<ref name= BB100/> The pastures contain breeding [[northern lapwing]]s, and species such as [[sedge warbler|sedge]] and [[Eurasian reed warbler|reed warblers]] and [[bearded tit]]s are found in patches of [[phragmites|common reed]].<ref name=walk>{{cite web |title=Coastal wildlife walk Blakeney Freshes, Norfolk |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/file/store5/item383877/version1/w-blakeney-blakeney_freshes-walk.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121119125933/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/file/store5/item383877/version1/w-blakeney-blakeney_freshes-walk.pdf |archive-date=19 November 2012 |url-status=dead |publisher=National Trust }} Retrieved 16 September 2012.</ref>

The Point juts into the sea on a north-facing coast, which means that [[bird migration|migrant birds]] may be found in spring and autumn, sometimes in huge numbers when the weather conditions force them towards land.<ref>Elkins (1988) pp. 136–137.</ref><ref>Newton (2010) pp. 97–98.</ref> Numbers are relatively low in spring, but autumn can produce large "falls", such as the hundreds of [[European robin]]s on 1 October 1951 or more than 400 [[common redstart]]s, on 18 September 1995. The common birds are regularly accompanied by scarcer species like [[greenish warbler]]s, [[great grey shrike]]s or [[Richard's pipit]]s. [[Seabird]]s may be sighted passing the Point, and migrating waders feed on the marshes at this time of year.<ref name= BB100/> [[vagrant species|Vagrant rarities]] have turned up when the weather is appropriate,<ref>Newton (2010) p. 50.</ref> including a [[Fea's petrel|Fea's]] or [[Zino's petrel]] in 1997, a [[trumpeter finch]] in 2008, and an [[alder flycatcher]] in 2010. [[Ornithology|Ornithologist]] and pioneering bird photographer [[Emma Turner (photographer)|Emma Turner]] started [[bird ringing|ringing]] common terns on the Point in 1909, and the use of this technique for migration studies has continued since. A notable recovery was a Sandwich tern killed for food in Angola, and a [[Radde's warbler]] trapped for ringing in 1961 was only the second British record of this species at that time.<ref name= BB100/> In the winter, the marshes hold [[European golden plover|golden plover]]s and [[wildfowl]] including [[common shelduck]], [[Eurasian wigeon]], [[brant goose|brent geese]] and [[common teal]],<ref name = walk/> while [[common scoter]]s, [[common eider]]s, [[common goldeneye]]s and [[red-breasted merganser]]s swim offshore.<ref>Allison (1989) pp. 87–88.</ref>

===Other animals===
[[File:Athalia rosae 2006.08.12 15.36.24-p8120093.jpg|alt= mainly orange fly|The [[turnip sawfly]] sometimes appears in huge numbers.|thumb]]
Blakeney Point has a mixed colony of about 500 [[Harbor seal|harbour]] and [[grey seal]]s. The harbour seals have their young between June and August, and the pups, which can swim almost immediately, may be seen on the mud flats. Grey seals breed in winter, between November and January; their young cannot swim until they have lost their first white coat, so they are restricted to dry land for their first three or four weeks, and can be viewed on the beach during this period.<ref name=DK/> Grey seals colonised a site in east Norfolk in 1993, and started breeding regularly at Blakeney in 2001. It is possible that they now outnumber harbour seals off the Norfolk coast.<ref name=Skeate>{{cite journal|last=Skeate |first=Eleanor R |author2=Perrow, Martin R |author3=Gilroy, James J |year=2012 |title=Likely effects of construction of Scroby Sands offshore wind farm on a mixed population of harbour ''Phoca vitulina'' and grey ''Halichoerus grypus'' seals |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |volume=64 |pages=872–881 |doi=10.1016/j.marpolbul.2012.01.029 |pmid=22333892 |issue=4 |bibcode=2012MarPB..64..872S }}</ref> Seal-watching boat trips run from Blakeney and Morston harbours, giving good views without disturbing the seals.<ref name=DK/> The corpses of 24 female or juvenile harbour seals were found in the Blakeney area between March 2009 and August 2010, each with spirally cut wounds consistent with the animal having been drawn through a [[ducted propeller]].<ref name = mru>Thompson ''et al'' (2010) pp. 1–4.</ref>

The [[European rabbit|rabbit]] population can grow to a level at which their grazing and burrowing adversely affects the fragile dune vegetation. When rabbit numbers are reduced by [[myxomatosis]], the plants recover, although those that are toxic to rabbits, like [[Jacobaea vulgaris|ragwort]], then become less common due to increased competition from the edible species.<ref name= elton>Elton (1979) pp. 167–168.</ref><ref name= white>{{cite journal| last= White | first= D J B| year=1961 | title= Some observations on the vegetation of Blakeney Point, Norfolk, following the disappearance of the rabbits in 1954 | journal= Journal of Ecology | volume= 49 | issue = 1 | pages= 113–118 | doi =10.2307/2257428 | jstor= 2257428| bibcode= 1961JEcol..49..113W}}</ref> The rabbits may be killed by [[carnivore]]s such as red foxes, weasels and stoats.<ref name= BB100/> Records of mammals that are rare in the NNR area include [[red deer]] swimming in the haven, a [[European hedgehog|hedgehog]] and a beached [[Sowerby's beaked whale]].<ref name=guardian>{{Cite news |last=Barkham |first=Patrick |title=Do we still need nature reserves? |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London |date=24 August 2012 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2012/aug/24/blakeney-point-coastal-nature-reserve-centenary |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008160334/http://www.guardian.co.uk/environment/2012/aug/24/blakeney-point-coastal-nature-reserve-centenary |archive-date=8 October 2012 |url-status=live }} Retrieved 16 September 2012.</ref>

An insect survey in September 2009 recorded 187 beetle species, including two new to Norfolk, the [[rove beetle]] ''[[Phytosus nigriventris]]'' and the [[Cucujoidea|fungus beetle]] ''[[Leiodes ciliaris]]'', and two very rarely seen in the county, the [[sap beetle]] ''[[Nitidula carnaria]]'' and the [[Histeridae|clown beetle]] ''[[Gnathoncus nanus]]''. There were also 24 types of spider, and the five ant species included the nationally rare'' [[Myrmica specioides]]''.<ref name=bbc>{{cite news |title=Rare beetles found at Blakeney National Nature Reserve |work=BBC Norfolk |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/local/norfolk/hi/people_and_places/nature/newsid_8516000/8516903.stm |publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation |location=Norwich Retrieved 16 September 2012.</ref> The rare [[millipede]] ''[[Thalassisobates littoralis]]'', a specialist of coastal shingle habitats, was found here in 1972,<ref name= Blower>Blower (1985) pp. 98–101.</ref> and a [[red-veined darter]] appeared in 2012.<ref name=atropos>{{cite web |title=Migrant insect summary – end of June 2012 Study Group |url=http://www.record-lrc.co.uk/Downloads/Sawfly%20Study%20Group%20Newsletter%202%5B14032009%5D.pdf |page=11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005011604/http://www.record-lrc.co.uk/Downloads/Sawfly%20Study%20Group%20Newsletter%202%5B14032009%5D.pdf |archive-date=5 October 2013 |url-status=live |access-date=24 September 2012 }}</ref> The [[silver Y]] moth also appears in large numbers in some years.<ref name = AM79>Foster, W A in Allison & Morley (1989) p. 79.</ref>

The many inhabitants of the tidal flats include [[lugworm]]s, [[polychaete|polychaete worms]], [[Talitrus saltator|sand hoppers]] and other [[amphipoda|amphipod crustaceans]], and [[gastropoda|gastropod molluscs]]. These [[mollusca|molluscs]] feed on the [[algae]] growing on the surface of the mud, and include the tiny ''[[Hydrobia ulvae|Hydrobia]]'', an important food for waders because of its abundance at densities of more than 130,000 m<sup>−2</sup>. [[Bivalvia|Bivalve molluscs]] include the edible [[Cerastoderma edule|common cockle]], although it is not harvested here.<ref name = AM67>Barnes, R S K in Allison & Morley (1989) pp. 67–75.</ref>

===Plants===
[[File:Salicornia europaea MS 0802.JPG|alt=green fleshy plant|thumb|Samphire, an edible plant]]
Grasses such as [[Agropyron pungens|sea couch grass]] and [[Puccinellia maritima|sea poa grass]] have an important function in the driest areas of the marshes, and on the coastal dunes, where [[Ammophila arenaria|marram grass]], [[Elymus farctus|sand couch-grass]], [[Leymus arenarius|lyme-grass]] and [[Corynephorus canescens|grey hair-grass]] help to bind the sand. [[Eryngium maritimum|Sea holly]], [[Carex arenaria|sand sedge]], [[Lotus corniculatus|bird's-foot trefoil]] and [[pyramidal orchid]] are other specialists of this arid habitat.<ref name = NNR/><ref name = encitation/> Some specialised [[moss]]es and [[lichen]]s are found on the dunes, and help to consolidate the sand;<ref name= Tansley855>Tansley (1939) p. 855.</ref> a survey in September 2009 found 41 lichen species.<ref name = bbc/> The plant distribution is influenced by the dunes' age as well as their moisture content, the deposits becoming less alkaline as [[calcium carbonate]] from animal shells is leached out of the sand to be replaced by more acidic [[humus]] from plant decomposition products. Marram grass is particularly discouraged by the change in acidity.<ref name= gorham>{{cite journal| last= Gorham | first= Eville | year= 1958| title= Soluble salts in dune sands from Blakeney Point in Norfolk | journal= Journal of Ecology | volume= 46 | issue = 2 | pages= 373–379 | doi =10.2307/2257401 | jstor= 2257401 | bibcode= 1958JEcol..46..373G }}</ref> A similar pattern is seen with [[bryophyte|mosses]] and lichens, with the various areas of the dunes containing different species according to the acidity of the sand.<ref name= richards/> At least four moss species have been identified as important in dune stabilization, since they help to consolidate the sand, add nutrients as they decompose, and pave the way for more exacting plant species.<ref name = AM60>Lodge, E in Allison & Morley (1989) pp. 60–63.</ref> The moss and lichen flora of Blakeney Point differs markedly from that of lime-rich dunes on the western coasts of the UK.<ref name= richards>{{cite journal| last= Richards | first= P W| year=1929 | title= Notes on the ecology of the bryophytes and lichens at Blakeney Point, Norfolk | journal= Journal of Ecology | volume= 17| issue = 1 | pages= 127–140 | doi =10.2307/2255917 | jstor= 2255917| bibcode= 1929JEcol..17..127R}}</ref> [[introduced species|Non-native]] [[lupinus arboreus|tree lupins]] have become established near the Lifeboat House, where they now grow wild.<ref name = AM41>White, D J B in Allison & Morley (1989) p. 41.</ref><ref name = mabey>Mabey (1996) p. 226.</ref>

The shingle ridge attracts [[Sedum acre|biting stonecrop]], [[Silene maritima|sea campion]], [[Glaucium flavum|yellow horned poppy]], [[Armeria maritima|sea thrift]], bird's foot trefoil and [[sea beet]].<ref name = encitation/> In the damper areas, where the shingle adjoins salt marsh, [[Limonium binervosum|rock sea lavender]], [[Limonium bellidifolium|matted sea lavender]] and [[Suaeda vera|scrubby sea-blite]] also thrive, although they are scarce in Britain away from the Norfolk coast.<ref name = NNR/> The saltmarsh contains [[Salicornia europaea|European glasswort]] and [[Spartina anglica|common cord grass]] in the most exposed regions, with a succession of plants following on as the marsh becomes more established: first [[Aster tripolium|sea aster]], then mainly sea lavender, with [[Halimione portulacoides|sea purslane]] in the creeks, and smaller areas of [[Plantago maritima|sea plantain]] and other common marsh plants.<ref name = encitation/>  Six previously unknown [[diatom]] species were found in the waters around the point in 1952, along with six others not previously recorded in Britain.<ref name= Salah>{{cite journal| last= Salah  | first= M M | year=1952 | title= Diatoms from Blakeney Point, Norfolk. New Species and new records for Great Britain | journal= Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society | volume=  72 | issue = 3 | pages= 156–169 | doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2818.1952.tb01971.x | pmid= 13023750 }}</ref>

European glasswort is picked between May and September and sold locally as "samphire".<ref name= Stannard>Stannard & Smith (2005) p. 34</ref> It is a fleshy plant which when blanched or steamed has a taste which leads to its alternative name of "sea asparagus", and it is often eaten with fish.<ref name= Knights>Knights & Phillips (1979) p. 49.</ref><ref name= Sweetser>Sweetser & Laurie (2009) p. 187.</ref> It can also be eaten raw when young.<ref name=guardian2>{{Cite news |last=Fearnley-Whittingstall |first=Hugh |title=Join the samphire brigade |newspaper=The Guardian |location=London |date=June 2007 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2007/jun/30/features.weekend |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120621215428/http://www.guardian.co.uk/lifeandstyle/2007/jun/30/features.weekend |archive-date=21 June 2012 |url-status=live }} Retrieved 21 October 2012.</ref> Glasswort is also a favourite food for the rabbits, which will venture onto the saltmarsh in search of this succulent plant.<ref name= rowan>{{cite journal| last= Rowan | first= William | year=1913 | title= Note on the food plants of rabbits on Blakeney Point, Norfolk | journal = Journal of Ecology | volume= 1 | issue = 4 | pages = 273–274 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1449448| doi =10.2307/2255570 | jstor= 2255570 | bibcode= 1913JEcol...1..273R }}</ref>

==Recreation==
[[File:Seals Blakeney Point.jpg|thumb|alt= seals on sea-washed sand|Seals at the Point can be viewed from boats from Morston.]]
The 7.7 million day visitors and 5.5 million who made overnight stays on the Norfolk coast in 1999 are estimated to have spent £122 million, and secured the equivalent of 2,325 full-time jobs in that area. A 2005 survey at six North Norfolk coastal sites, including Blakeney, Cley and Morston found that 39 per cent of visitors gave [[birdwatching]] as the main purpose of their visit.<ref name =liley4/> The villages nearest to the Point, Blakeney and Cley, had the highest ''per capita'' spend per visitor of those surveyed, and Cley was one of the two sites with the highest proportion of pre-planned visits. The equivalent of 52 full-time jobs in the Cley and Blakeney area are estimated to result from the £2.45 million spent locally by the visiting public.<ref>{{cite web |title=Valuing Norfolk's Coast |url=http://www.rspb.org.uk/Images/Valuing_norfolks_coast_tcm9-203973.pdf |publisher=Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304002056/http://www.rspb.org.uk/Images/Valuing_norfolks_coast_tcm9-203973.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 |url-status=live }} Retrieved 29 June 2012.</ref> In addition to birdwatching and boat trips to see the seals, [[sailing]] and walking are the other significant [[tourism|tourist activities]] in the area.<ref name = walk/><ref name= pevsner394/>

The large number of visitors at coastal sites sometimes has negative effects. Wildlife may be disturbed, a frequent difficulty for species that breed in exposed areas such as ringed plovers and little terns, and also for wintering geese.<ref name =liley10/> During the breeding season, the main breeding areas for terns and seals are fenced off and signposted.<ref name = NTwalk/> Plants can be trampled, which is a particular problem in sensitive habitats such as sand dunes and vegetated shingle.<ref name =liley10>Liley (2008) pp. 10–14.</ref> A boardwalk made from recycled plastic crosses the large sand dunes near the end of the Point, which helps to reduce erosion.<ref name = NTwalk/> It was installed in 2009 at a cost of £35,000 to replace its much less durable wooden predecessor.<ref name= view>{{cite journal | last= Wood | first= David | year= 2009 | title= A new boardwalk on Blakeney Point | journal= Views | volume= 46  | page= 58 | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/file/store5/item699376/version1/w-autumn-2009.pdf#page=59 }}{{dead link|date=May 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Dogs are not allowed from April to mid-August because of the risk to ground-nesting birds, and must be on a lead or closely controlled at other times.<ref name=NTwalk>{{cite web |title=Blakeney Point coastal walk to Lifeboat House |work=Blakeney National Nature Reserve, Morston, Norfolk |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/pdf/1/530033/Trail/Walking/Blakeney_Point_coastal_walk_to_Lifeboat_House.pdf |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/6BEUm5TVN?url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/pdf/1/530033/Trail/Walking/Blakeney_Point_coastal_walk_to_Lifeboat_House.pdf |archive-date=7 October 2012 |url-status=dead |publisher=National Trust }} Retrieved 13 September 2012.</ref>

The Norfolk Coast Partnership, a grouping of conservation and environmental bodies, divide the coast and its [[hinterland]] into three zones for tourism development purposes. Blakeney Point, along with [[Holme Dunes]] and [[Holkham National Nature Reserve|Holkham dunes]], is considered to be a sensitive habitat already suffering from visitor pressure, and therefore designated as a red-zone area with no development or parking improvements to be recommended. The rest of the reserve is placed in the orange zone, for locations with fragile habitats but less tourism pressure.<ref name= zones>Scott Wilson Ltd (2006) pp. 5–6.</ref>

==Coastal changes==
[[File:The Shingle spit.jpg|alt= long ridge of shingle|The shingle ridge is moving southwards through the marshes.|thumb]]
The spit is a relatively young feature in [[geology|geological]] terms, and in recent centuries it has been extending westwards and landwards through tidal and storm action.<ref name = NNR/> This growth is thought to have been enhanced by the reclamation of the salt marshes along this coast in recent centuries, which removed a natural barrier to the movement of shingle.<ref name= smp532>East Anglia Coastal Group (2010) pp. 13–14.</ref> The amount of shingle moved by a single storm can be "spectacular";<ref name = NNR>{{cite web| title= Blakeney Point National Nature Reserve| url= http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/Images/Blakeneypoint_tcm6-22495.pdf| publisher= Natural England}} Retrieved 23 November 2011.</ref><ref name = BB100/> the spit has sometimes been breached, becoming an island for a time, and this may happen again.<ref name="wrightchap"/><ref name =may>May, V J (2003) "[http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/pdf/gcrdb/GCRsiteaccount2038.pdf North Norfolk Coast]" in May (2003) pp. 1–19.</ref> The northernmost part of Snitterley (now Blakeney) village was lost to the sea in the early Middle Ages, probably due to a storm.<ref name= muir>Muir (2008) p. 103.</ref> In the last two hundred years, maps have been accurate enough for the distance from the Blakeney Chapel ruins to the sea to be measured. The {{convert|400|m|yd|abbr=on}} in 1817 had become {{convert|320|m|yd|abbr=on}} by 1835, {{convert|275|m|yd|abbr=on}} in 1907, and {{convert|195|m|yd|abbr=on}} by the end of the 20th century.<ref name= wrightchap/> The spit is moving towards the mainland at about {{convert|1|m|yd|abbr=on}} per year;<ref name= gray>Gray (2004) pp. 363–365.</ref> and several former raised islands or "eyes" have already disappeared, first covered by the advancing shingle, and then lost to the sea.<ref name=carnell/> The massive [[North Sea flood of 1953|1953 flood]] overran the main beach, and only the highest dune tops remained above water. Sand was washed into the salt marshes, and the extreme tip of the point was breached, but as with other purely natural parts of the coast, like Scolt Head Island, little lasting damage was done.<ref name = AM7>Allison H & Morley J in Allison & Morley (1989) pp. 7–8.</ref>

Landward movement of the shingle meant that the channel of the Glaven was becoming blocked increasingly often by 2004. This led to flooding of Cley village and the environmentally important Blakeney freshwater marshes.<ref name=carnell>{{cite journal | last= Carnell | first= Peter | year= 1999 | title= The chapel on Blakeney Eye: initial results of field surveys | journal= Glaven Historian | volume= 2 | url= http://www.history-blakeney-area.org.uk/GH-Files/GH1-5/GH%202.7.pdf | pages= 34–45 | access-date= 2013-12-01 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131203023815/http://www.history-blakeney-area.org.uk/GH-Files/GH1-5/GH%202.7.pdf | archive-date= 2013-12-03 | url-status= dead }}</ref> The [[Environment Agency]] considered several remedial options. It concluded that attempting to hold back the shingle or breaching the spit to create a new outlet for the Glaven would be expensive and probably ineffective, and doing nothing would be environmentally damaging.<ref name= gray/> The Agency decided to create a new route for the river to the south of its original line,<ref name= murphy/> and work to realign a {{convert|550|m|yd|abbr=on}} stretch of river {{convert|200|m|yd|abbr=on}} further south was completed in 2007 at a cost of about £1.5 million.<ref name=defra>{{cite web |title=Case Study Report 2 Blakeney Freshes River Glaven Realignment and Cley to Salthouse Drainage Improvements |work=Coastal Schemes with Multiple Funders and Objectives FD2635 |url=http://randd.defra.gov.uk/Document.aspx?Document=CaseStudy2BlakeneyFreshesRGlavenRealignmentFD2635.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121009071404/http://randd.defra.gov.uk/Document.aspx?Document=CaseStudy2BlakeneyFreshesRGlavenRealignmentFD2635.pdf |archive-date=9 October 2012 |url-status=live |publisher=Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), Environment Agency, Maslem Environmental }} Retrieved 4 December 2011.</ref> The Glaven had previously been realigned from an earlier, more northerly, course in 1922.<ref name=carnell/> The ruins of Blakeney Chapel are now to the north of the river embankment, and essentially unprotected from coastal erosion, since the advancing [[shingle beach|shingle]] will no longer be swept away by the stream. The chapel will be buried by a ridge of shingle as the spit continues to move south, and then lost to the sea,<ref name=helm>{{cite web |title=Blakeney Chapel SAM (Scheduled Ancient Monument), North Norfolk |work=HELM (Historic Environment Local Management) |url=http://www.helm.org.uk/server/show/ConCaseStudy.97 |publisher=English Heritage |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120809085524/http://www.helm.org.uk/server/show/ConCaseStudy.97 |archive-date=9 August 2012 |url-status=live }} Retrieved 19 September 2011.</ref> perhaps within 20–30 years.<ref name= murphy>Murphy (2009) p. 9.</ref>

'''Denton Castle''' is a [[motte and bailey]] castle built in the village of [[Denton, Norfolk|Denton]], [[Norfolk]], England.

==History==
[[Image:Denton Castle.jpg|thumb|left|1884 plan and cross-section of Denton Castle]]
Denton Castle was built after 1088, following the [[Norman invasion of England]], probably by William d'Albini, who linked his estate at Denton to that at [[Buckenham]], where he also built a [[Buckenham Castle|castle]].<ref>''[http://www.heritage.norfolk.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MNF11047 Norfolk Historic Environmental Record No. 11047]'', Norfolk Heritage Explorer, accessed 28 June 2011; Manning, p.342.</ref> The motte is around 150 feet in diameter, surrounded by a protective ditch, with an adjacent, horseshoe-shaped bailey.<ref>Manning, p.336.</ref> The castle may have been destroyed around 1254.<ref name=HER>''[http://www.heritage.norfolk.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MNF11047 Norfolk Historic Environmental Record No. 11047]'', Norfolk Heritage Explorer, accessed 28 June 2011.</ref>

Today the castle is a [[scheduled monument]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1003994|desc=Castle Hill, Hangman's Hill and adjoining earthworks, Darrow Green}}</ref> It was purchased by the [[National Trust]] in 1990 and forms part of the Trust's Darrow Wood pasture.<ref>National Trust, [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/darrow-wood#Overview Darrow Wood: Overview], accessed 29 December 2018</ref>
